n: Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection and AIDS

faq.a: A negative rapid test is reliable if the patient is beyond the window period (≥4 weeks post‑exposure); otherwise repeat testing.
faq.q: Can a negative rapid test rule out HIV?

faq.a: Viral load directly measures replication; a rise indicates treatment failure before CD4 falls.
faq.q: Why is viral load preferred to CD4 for monitoring treatment?

faq.a: Trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole, started when CD4 drops below 200 cells/µL.
faq.q: What is the first drug to give for PCP prophylaxis?

exam: A 32‑year‑old woman presents with chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and oral thrush. Which investigation confirms HIV and what is the next step? — Perform a rapid antibody test; if positive, start confirmatory ELISA and begin cART promptly.
How does WHO stage 3 differ from stage 4 HIV infection? — Stage 3 has CD4 200‑349 cells/µL or moderate opportunistic disease; stage 4 has CD4 <200 cells/µL or AIDS‑defining illness.

A patient on tenofovir‑based cART develops rising creatinine. What alternative regimen is appropriate in a low‑resource setting? — Switch to abacavir‑based regimen if HLA‑B*57:01 negative, avoiding nephrotoxic drugs.
Why is isoniazid preventive therapy recommended for all HIV patients in East Africa, even without active TB? — High TB prevalence; latent infection can progress rapidly in immunosuppressed hosts.
What clinical feature distinguishes Kaposi sarcoma from other skin lesions in HIV patients? — Violaceous, non‑painful plaques or nodules on the skin or mucosa, often on lower extremities.

A patient with CD4 180 cells/µL presents with cough and night sweats. Which test should you order first and why? — Sputum GeneXpert for TB; TB is the leading cause of mortality in HIV and requires early treatment.
Explain why a high viral load despite good adherence suggests drug resistance. — Persistent replication indicates the virus has mutated; requires resistance testing and regimen change.

What immediate management is required for an HIV‑positive patient with new onset seizures? — Assess for cryptococcal meningitis (lumbar puncture, India ink) and start empiric antifungal therapy while arranging CSF analysis.
ai.title: Human Immunodeficiency Virus Infection and AIDS
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: HIV infection progresses through defined stages to AIDS, causing immune collapse and opportunistic disease. Diagnosis relies on serology and viral load, while management combines antiretroviral therapy and prevention of complications, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: HIV infection confirmed by a positive rapid antibody test plus a confirmatory ELISA or Western blot.
AIDS diagnosed when CD4 <200 cells/µL or WHO stage 4 condition occurs.
sections.p: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is a retrovirus that infects CD4+ T‑cells, leading to progressive immunodeficiency. AIDS is the clinical syndrome defined by a CD4 count <200 cells/µL or the presence of specific opportunistic infections or cancers.

b: Stage 1: CD4 ≥500 cells/µL, no symptoms.
Stage 2: CD4 350‑499 cells/µL, mild mucocutaneous manifestations.
Stage 3: CD4 200‑349 cells/µL, moderate opportunistic disease.
Stage 4: CD4 <200 cells/µL or AIDS‑defining illness.
sections.p: The WHO clinical staging system (1–4) and CD4 count guide severity. Stage 1 is asymptomatic; stage 4 includes AIDS‑defining illnesses.

b: Unprotected vaginal or anal intercourse.
Contaminated needles (e.g., unsafe injections).
Mother‑to‑child during pregnancy, delivery, or breastfeeding.
sections.p: HIV is transmitted through blood, sexual contact, and perinatal routes. In East Africa, heterosexual transmission and mother‑to‑child spread dominate.

b: Acute retroviral syndrome (2‑4 weeks after exposure).
Weight loss >10 % of body weight.
Recurrent oral thrush, chronic diarrhoea, or persistent fever.
sections.p: Early infection may be asymptomatic or cause a flu‑like illness. Chronic infection leads to weight loss, chronic diarrhoea, persistent fever, lymphadenopathy, and opportunistic infections such as TB, cryptococcal meningitis, or Kaposi sarcoma.
Testing must answer whether infection is present, how far immune function has declined, and whether opportunistic disease is present.

t.b: Is the patient infected? – Positive indicates exposure; requires confirmatory test.
What is immune status? – <200 cells/µL defines AIDS; guides prophylaxis.
How active is replication? – High load suggests treatment failure; not always available, use clinical staging if absent.

t.a: Full blood count, liver function, renal function
t.b: Baseline organ status before ART; abnormalities may affect drug choice.

t.a: Chest X‑ray, sputum GeneXpert for TB
t.b: Is TB co‑infection present? – Common in low‑resource settings; treat concurrently.

b: Opportunistic infections: TB, cryptococcal meningitis, PCP pneumonia.
Cancers: Kaposi sarcoma, non‑Hodgkin lymphoma.
Neurological decline: HIV‑associated dementia.
Severe anaemia or renal failure from ART.
sections.p: Complications arise from severe immunosuppression and drug toxicity.

b: cART (e.g., tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir) – suppresses viral replication, restores CD4.
Trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis when CD4 <200 cells/µL – prevents PCP and toxoplasmosis.
Isoniazid preventive therapy for latent TB in high‑TB prevalence areas.
Treat active opportunistic infections according to local protocols; avoid steroids unless indicated.
sections.p: First line is lifelong combination antiretroviral therapy (cART). Supportive care prevents and treats opportunistic disease.

b: Clinic visit every 3 months for clinical review and labs.
Adherence counseling – missed doses lead to resistance.
Partner testing and treatment.
Neonatal prophylaxis with nevirapine for infants of HIV‑positive mothers.
sections.p: Regular monitoring of CD4, viral load (if available), and drug toxicity is essential. Prevention includes counseling, condom provision, and PMTCT (prevention of mother‑to‑child transmission).

b: Tuberculosis alone – common co‑infection; differentiate by sputum testing.
Chronic malaria with splenomegaly – may cause anaemia but does not cause CD4 loss.
Lymphoma – can present with lymphadenopathy and weight loss; biopsy required.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic HIV‑related wasting or opportunistic disease.

b: CD4 count can be transiently high during acute infection – rely on clinical stage.
Serology for hepatitis B may be negative if immune system is severely suppressed.
Chest X‑ray may miss early TB; use GeneXpert when possible.
sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal or abnormal in advanced HIV.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid weight loss >10 % in a month
